coverage_limits: OpenAlex hit its anonymous daily credit limit (HTTP 429, retry after about 5.5 hours) after two queries, so I could not run the planned citing-work passes on the anchor papers (Hao et al. 2026, Kusumegi et al. 2025, Liang et al. 2024 and 2025, Qian et al. 2026). The arXiv API also rate-limited for about 30 minutes, so some passes used arXiv search pages. SSRN and NBER were reached only through Crossref and web search, and the journal passes used Crossref keyword search capped at 25 to 60 rows per journal. No full texts were read: every design and question guess rests on the abstract, and sample sizes are given only where the abstract states them. For recall, I kept several AI-versus-human comparisons and some finds outside the science lane (education, marketing, software). Measurement-only studies are limited to six prominent ones (design 'other'). This run covered the obs-science search lane only. It did not touch the separate request to download the 38 experiments without full text, which RESUME.md shows was handled with tools/open_missing.py.

candidates.title: Research Novelty in Information Systems Journals After ChatGPT: Differences Across Institutional Language Contexts
candidates.task: Information Systems journal articles (13,847 abstracts, 2020-2025)
candidates.evidence: Compares SPECTER2 semantic novelty (distance from nearest recent predecessors) of articles in 44 IS journals before and after ChatGPT; articles with first authors in non-English-dominant countries show a 0.176 SD larger post-2022 decline in relative novelty. Individual LLM use is not observed; v1 carried the title 'Do Large Language Models Reduce Research Novelty? Evidence from Information Systems Journals'.

candidates.title: How Did Writing Change At CHI? Analyzing 44 Years of CHI Writing Before and After the Introduction of Large Language Models
candidates.task: CHI conference papers (14,262 full texts, 1982-2026)
candidates.evidence: Tracks readability, register, lexical diversity and LLM marker words across all CHI proceedings and tests whether academic prose homogenized after LLMs; finds no homogenization, more varied vocabulary, and an existing shift that LLMs accelerated rather than started.

candidates.title: Divergent LLM Adoption and Heterogeneous Convergence Paths in Research Writing
candidates.task: arXiv papers (over 627,000) with detected ChatGPT-revision style
candidates.evidence: Detects ChatGPT-revised style in arXiv manuscripts and uses difference-in-differences to show LLM use drives convergence in academic writing, with early adopters, male, non-native and junior researchers moving most toward the style of established researchers.

candidates.title: LLM assisted writing deserves empirical evaluation
candidates.task: Health informatics papers (69,209)
candidates.evidence: Links estimated LLM-assisted writing in health informatics papers to a more focused topical and semantic presentation (fewer topics per paper, embeddings closer to topic centroids), broader citation practices, and more globally distributed authorship.

candidates.title: More of the same? Are scientific papers losing originality?
candidates.task: Full-text papers in CORE across eight fields (over 26,000, 2015-2025)
candidates.evidence: Measures the share of each paper's text that semantically resembles recent prior work (against a fixed-size comparison sample); the share was stable before 2021 and more than tripled by 2025, with a similar rise in passages restating the same idea. The abstract does not attribute the change to LLMs, so the generative-AI link rests on timing only.

candidates.title: AI-assisted writing and the reorganization of scientific knowledge
candidates.task: About 2 million full-text research articles (2021-2024) linked to citation networks
candidates.evidence: Relates the share of LLM-like text in a paper to disruption, cross-field citation breadth and citation concentration in within-author, within-field models; after 2023, higher AI-assisted writing intensity goes with more disruption but no broader knowledge sourcing.

candidates.title: Return of the solo author: The changing division of labor in science in the age of generative AI
candidates.task: Over 300 million works across 26 fields
candidates.evidence: Finds the long decline in solo authorship halted and partly reversed after ChatGPT; solo papers by authors who had only published in teams narrow in scope and shift toward computational topics. The main outcome is team structure, so the scope-narrowing result is the only diversity-related outcome (borderline).

candidates.title: Impact of large language models on peer review opinions from a fine-grained perspective: evidence from top conference proceedings in AI
candidates.task: Peer review reports at top AI conferences
candidates.evidence: Compares review reports before and after LLMs and flags likely LLM-modified reviews; post-LLM reviews are longer and more fluent, use more standardized language (especially low-confidence reviewers), and attend less to originality and deeper evaluative aspects.

candidates.title: Do LLMs Favor LLMs? Quantifying Interaction Effects in Peer Review
candidates.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency (FAccT)
candidates.task: Over 125,000 paper-review pairs from ICLR, NeurIPS and ICML
candidates.evidence: Studies LLM-assisted papers and LLM-assisted reviews jointly; LLM-assisted reviews are more lenient toward weaker papers, and fully LLM-generated reviews show severe rating compression. There is no content-diversity outcome, so this is borderline peer-review evidence.

candidates.title: LLM-as-a-Reviewer: Benchmarking Their Ability, Divergence, and Prompt Injection Resistance as Paper Reviewers
candidates.task: LLM-generated vs human reviews for 898 NeurIPS and ICLR papers
candidates.evidence: Benchmarks 12 LLMs as reviewers against human reviews; LLMs overrate weaker papers, diverge from humans in topical emphasis, and write reviews two to three times longer with lower lexical diversity and more standardized vocabulary. A related earlier paper by an overlapping team (arXiv 2509.09912) is listed separately.

candidates.title: When Your Reviewer is an LLM: Biases, Divergence, and Prompt Injection Risks in Peer Review
candidates.authors: Zhu, Xiong, Ma, Lu, Liu, Li
candidates.task: GPT-5-mini vs human reviews for 1,441 ICLR 2023 and NeurIPS 2022 papers
candidates.evidence: Compares LLM-generated and human reviews on ratings, strengths and weaknesses using topic modeling and similarity analysis, and tests prompt injection; LLMs inflate ratings for weaker papers. Diversity is not a main outcome (borderline). The SSRN versions were seen only in OpenAlex listings.

candidates.title: Large Language Models in Peer Review: Decision Alignment, Review-Text Characteristics, and Human–AI Aggregation at ICLR 2025
candidates.task: 2,401 human vs 7,203 LLM reviews of ICLR 2025 submissions
candidates.evidence: Compares human reviews with reviews from Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-5.2 and Gemini 3 Pro; raw LLM scores show leniency and score compression, and review-text indicators show similar structural completeness. Borderline: it measures score dispersion but not content diversity.

candidates.title: PRAIB: Peer Review AI Benchmark of Behaviour of LLM-Assisted Reviewing
candidates.task: 11,000 LLM-generated vs human reviews for 1,000 ICLR and NeurIPS papers (2021-2025)
candidates.evidence: Machine-generated reviews diverge from human feedback: LLM ratings are less variable, positively biased and overconfident, and reviews are longer and more complex but often miss the specific weaknesses humans raise.

candidates.title: Stop Automating Peer Review Without Rigorous Evaluation
candidates.task: Human vs AI-generated reviews of ICLR 2026 submissions
candidates.evidence: Position paper built on an empirical comparison of human and AI-generated ICLR 2026 reviews: AI reviewers show a 'hivemind' of excessive agreement within and across papers that reduces perspective diversity, and LLM rewriting of papers games AI review scores.

candidates.title: Revolutionizing Peer Review: A Comparative Analysis of ChatGPT and Human Review Reports in Scientific Publishing
candidates.task: ChatGPT-4 vs human review reports for 198 manuscripts at the European Scientific Journal
candidates.evidence: Parallel AI and human reviews of the same manuscripts: ChatGPT-4 gave higher grades, mostly recommended minor revisions and never rejection, while human recommendations were more spread out. Borderline: only the dispersion of recommendations bears on diversity.

candidates.title: Can Large Language Models Provide Useful Feedback on Research Papers? A Large-Scale Empirical Analysis
candidates.task: GPT-4 vs human reviewer comments on Nature-family (3,096) and ICLR (1,709) papers
candidates.evidence: The overlap between points raised by GPT-4 and by human reviewers (30.85% Nature journals, 39.23% ICLR) is comparable to the overlap between two human reviewers; a separate user study of 308 researchers measured perceived helpfulness. Included as AI-versus-human similarity evidence in peer review (borderline).

candidates.title: Contemporary AI lacks the imagination to diverge or negate in science
candidates.authors: Bao, Wu, Liu, Li, Cao, Evans
candidates.task: LLM-generated ideas from authors' own preprints (121,640 invited) rated by scientists; 39 million papers 2010-2025
candidates.evidence: 6,749 scientists rated LLM ideas derived from their own papers: non-reasoning models collapse into a narrow 'hivemind' and no model proposes null hypotheses. An analysis of 39 million papers links ChatGPT's release to sharply suppressed null claims and contracting ideas. Mixed design: AI-output evaluation plus an observational corpus analysis.

candidates.title: The Ideation-Execution Gap: Execution Outcomes of LLM-Generated versus Human Research Ideas
candidates.venue: International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2026), poster
candidates.task: NLP researchers executing research ideas (over 100 hours each, 4-page papers)
candidates.evidence: 43 expert researchers were randomly assigned to execute either an LLM-generated or an expert-written idea; blind reviews before and after execution show LLM ideas' novelty, excitement, effectiveness and overall scores fall significantly more, erasing or reversing their ideation-stage lead. The assignment varies the idea's source, not AI help during the work.

candidates.title: When ChatGPT Writes Your Research Proposal: Scientific Creativity in the Age of Generative AI
candidates.task: Brief research proposals for a fictitious experimental-psychology scenario
candidates.evidence: ChatGPT-4 proposals (hypothesis, design, equipment, justification) were compared with graduate students' proposals, and two experts rated them blind for scientific creativity; ChatGPT scored higher overall and on originality and meaningfulness. The number of students is not given in the abstract.

candidates.title: Machine-assisted social psychology hypothesis generation
candidates.task: Social psychology research hypotheses
candidates.evidence: Experts rated hypotheses from a fine-tuned GPT-3 similar to human-generated ones on clarity, originality and impact, and rated GPT-4 hypotheses higher than human ones. Bibliographic data come from Crossref; the findings come from a search snippet of the abstract only.

candidates.title: Automating psychological hypothesis generation with AI: when large language models meet causal graph
candidates.task: Psychology hypotheses on well-being
candidates.evidence: 130 hypotheses from an LLM combined with a causal knowledge graph were compared with research ideas from doctoral scholars and with LLM-only hypotheses; the combined approach matched doctoral-level novelty and beat LLM-only hypotheses.

candidates.title: Artificial intelligences and human scientists exhibit complementary strengths in theory building
candidates.task: Social-science theory formulation, prediction and revision (gender and race inequality)
candidates.evidence: Compares 25 LLMs with 13 senior researchers and 60 doctoral scholars; AIs beat most individuals and their theories are rated higher quality, but human theories are more diverse and gain more from aggregation.

candidates.title: Measuring the Gap Between Human and LLM Research Ideas
candidates.task: Research ideas generated from the prior works that inspired published papers
candidates.evidence: LLM ideas generated from the same inspiring papers cluster around bridge-like opportunities and synthesis methods, while the human papers spread more broadly over a research-taste taxonomy. A comment (Dahl, arXiv 2609.15996) argues the published-paper baseline suffers from survivorship bias.

candidates.title: AI Research Agents Narrow Scientific Exploration
candidates.task: 219,655 ideas from five agent frameworks and five LLMs vs human-authored papers
candidates.evidence: AI-generated ideas are more concentrated than human-authored papers in the same research area, stay closer to the starting literature than human follow-on work, and align less with later human research.

candidates.title: Thinking Like a Scientist? A Structural Study of LLM-Generated Research Methods
candidates.task: Methodology suggestions for research questions from 1,000 arXiv computer-science papers
candidates.evidence: Methods suggested by GPT-5.1, Gemini 3 Pro and DeepSeek-V3.2 are compared with the methods the papers used; LLMs propose a much narrower set (effective number of models falls from 1,232 to 59-96), and inter-LLM correlations exceed LLM-to-paper correlations.

candidates.title: Large Language Models Reflect Human Citation Patterns with a Heightened Citation Bias
candidates.authors: Algaba, Mazijn, Holst, Tori, Wenmackers, Ginis
candidates.venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: NAACL 2025
candidates.task: LLM-suggested references for anonymized in-text citations in AAAI, NeurIPS, ICML and ICLR papers
candidates.evidence: References suggested by LLMs resemble human citation patterns but favor highly cited papers more strongly (an amplified Matthew effect), robust to controls for year, title length, author count and venue.

candidates.title: How deep do large language models internalize scientific literature and citation practices?
candidates.task: 274,951 GPT-4o-generated references for 10,000 papers vs ground-truth references
candidates.evidence: Generated references favor highly cited, more recent papers with shorter titles and smaller teams, reinforcing the Matthew effect relative to human reference lists, while staying semantically aligned with paper content.

candidates.title: When AI Writes, Who Gets Cited? Evidence of Citation Monoculture Across Language Models
candidates.task: Choosing up to ten papers from random panels of thirty real papers (120 papers)
candidates.evidence: Eleven LLMs from three vendors concentrate their picks sharply (top decile gets 23-30% of citations vs 15.6% under random choice) and share one preference map; eight domain experts choosing from the same blinded panels show no comparable shared preference.

candidates.title: Citing Less Critically: LLMs Reshape the Rhetoric and Reach of Scientific Citation
candidates.task: Masked-citation task on 1,746 NLP conference papers (63,000+ citation contexts)
candidates.evidence: Six LLMs regenerate citation sentences; compared with human citations they cite less critically, over-cite popular and older papers, and draw on more socially distant authors.

candidates.title: The Ideation Bottleneck: Decomposing the Quality Gap Between AI-Generated and Human Economics Research
candidates.task: 912 AI-generated economics papers (APE project) vs 41 human AER and AEJ: Policy papers
candidates.evidence: Splits the AI-human quality gap into idea quality (fine-tuned models trained on publication decisions) and execution quality (an LLM rubric); human papers lead on both, and the idea gap (d=2.23) explains about 71% of the difference. All measures are model-based, not human ratings.

candidates.title: Following the Crowd: Literature Support and the Capabilities of Autonomous Research Agents
candidates.venue: Graduate Institute of International and Development Studies, International Economics Department Working Paper No. HEIDWP14-2026
candidates.task: APE AI-generated economic policy papers vs human benchmark papers
candidates.evidence: Measures how crowded each paper's neighborhood is in the semantic space of economics abstracts; this literature support predicts tournament performance for AI-generated papers but not for human papers, so agents do better in well-trodden areas.

candidates.title: Recombination or Discovery? A Retrieval-Grounded Novelty Audit of Machine-Generated Research Papers
candidates.task: 166 machine-generated papers (FARS corpus) vs 166 topic-matched ICLR 2025 submissions
candidates.evidence: Splits papers into contribution claims and audits novelty against retrieved prior work; machine-generated contributions are labeled novel more often (56.1% vs 35.6%), but an adversarial re-audit overturns many verdicts, so LLM-judged novelty is treated as an upper bound.

candidates.title: All That Glitters is Not Novel: Plagiarism in AI Generated Research
candidates.venue: Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers)
candidates.task: Expert plagiarism audit of 50 LLM-generated research documents
candidates.evidence: 13 experts searched for overlap with existing work and found 24% of the LLM-generated research documents paraphrased or substantially borrowed, with most others showing some similarity. There is no human-generated comparison set; included because it challenges novelty ratings of AI research ideas.

candidates.title: Innovation or Imitation? A Critical Analysis of AI-Authored vs. Human-Authored Scientific Papers
candidates.venue: Proceedings of the 16th International Conference on Computer Supported Education (CSEDU 2024)
candidates.task: Scientific papers on three education and computing topics drafted by ChatGPT or Jenni AI vs human drafts
candidates.evidence: Qualitative comparison of AI-generated and human-written paper drafts; concludes that high-quality publications still need human input for depth, originality and rigor. Small qualitative study.

candidates.title: Fluent but Not Factual: A Comparative Analysis of ChatGPT and Other AI Chatbots’ Proficiency and Originality in Scientific Writing for Humanities
other_versions: arXiv 2309.08636 (titled 'ChatGPT v Bard v Bing v Claude 2 v Aria v human-expert. How good are AI chatbots at scientific writing?')
candidates.task: Scholarly writing in humanities and archaeology
candidates.evidence: Six chatbots are compared with a human expert on factual correctness and scientific contribution; all AIs merged existing knowledge well but none produced original scientific content.

candidates.title: Research Borderlands: Analysing Writing Across Research Cultures
candidates.venue: Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers)
candidates.task: Adapting research writing across research cultures (human papers vs LLM-generated text)
candidates.evidence: Builds metrics for structural, stylistic, rhetorical and citational norms from interviews with interdisciplinary researchers and applies them to human papers and LLM outputs; LLMs lack cultural competence and tend to homogenize writing across research cultures.

candidates.title: Does scientific writing converge to U.S. english? evidence from generative AI-assisted publications
candidates.task: 5.65 million English-language Scopus articles (2021-2024)
candidates.evidence: Event-study difference-in-differences around ChatGPT's release: GenAI-assisted publications from non-English-speaking countries grow increasingly similar (SciBERT embeddings) to a U.S. benchmark of scientific English relative to non-assisted publications.

candidates.title: Can We Still Trace L1 Signals? Investigating the Resilience of Native Language Signals in the LLM Era
candidates.task: Native-language identification on arXiv and ACL Anthology abstracts across three eras
candidates.evidence: Native-language identification accuracy on academic abstracts falls from the pre-neural to the pre-LLM to the post-LLM era, so academic English is homogenizing, though mostly before LLMs; rewriting experiments suggest LLM use could deepen it.

candidates.title: What Are LLMs Doing to Scientific Communication? Measuring Changes in Writing Practices and Reading Experience
candidates.venue: Proceedings of the Language Resources and Evaluation Conference (2026)
candidates.task: ACL Anthology papers 2020-2024 (over 37,000) plus 3,000 human passages and their LLM rewrites
candidates.evidence: Diachronic lexical and stylistic analysis shows LLM-modified texts use certain syntactic constructions, longer words and lower lexical diversity; 20 domain experts rated LLM-improved passages as more understandable and exciting.

candidates.title: Bridging Language Barriers: The Impact of Large Language Models on Academic Writing
candidates.task: Over one million arXiv abstracts by native and non-native English-speaking authors
candidates.evidence: Before-after comparison around ChatGPT's release: lexical diversity of native and non-native speakers converges and writing sophistication rises for all, most for non-native speakers.

candidates.title: The Behavioral Signature of GenAI in Scientific Communication
candidates.task: IZA discussion paper abstracts (economics)
candidates.evidence: Finds a stylistic shift after March 2023 in mean word length, type-token ratio and readability of economics working-paper abstracts, with growing convergence toward machine-generated writing. Largely a measurement study.

candidates.title: Have Large Language Models Enhanced the Way Civil & Environmental Engineers Write? A Quantitative Analysis of Scholarly Communication over 25 Years
candidates.task: 149,452 ASCE abstracts (2000-2025)
candidates.evidence: Vocabulary shifts point to LLM-assisted writing from 2023; abstracts classified as LLM-assisted show higher within-text lexical diversity and complexity. Mostly measurement, with no between-author diversity outcome.

candidates.title: Does GenAI Rewrite How We Write? An Empirical Study on Two-Million Preprints
candidates.task: 2.1 million preprints on arXiv, bioRxiv, medRxiv and SocArXiv (2016-2025)
candidates.evidence: Interrupted time series on volume, authorship, style and topics: LLMs sped up submission and revision, modestly raised linguistic complexity and disproportionately expanded AI-related topics. Only a topic-share shift bears on diversity (borderline).

candidates.title: AI Coding Agents in Social Science: Methodologically Diverse, Empirically Consistent, Interpretively Vulnerable
candidates.task: Many-analysts reanalysis of an immigration and social-policy question by Claude Code and Codex vs human teams
candidates.evidence: Twenty runs per agent are compared with a human many-analysts baseline: Codex matches human methodological diversity and Claude Code produces about three times as many specifications, while estimates stay near the human consensus.

candidates.title: Many AI Analysts, One Dataset: Navigating the Agentic Data Science Multiverse
candidates.task: Autonomous LLM analysts testing fixed hypotheses on three datasets
candidates.evidence: AI analysts reproduce the dispersion in effect sizes, p-values and conclusions seen in human many-analyst studies, and persona or model changes steer the results. The comparison to human analytic diversity is indirect (borderline).

candidates.title: The Agentic Garden of Forking Paths
candidates.task: AI agents reanalyzing a 42-team immigration many-analysts dataset and three other domains
candidates.evidence: Persona-conditioned agents reach divergent conclusions and reproduce 72% of the human ideological gap in effect estimates from the 42-team study. Borderline: about analytic dispersion rather than creativity.

candidates.title: The Hitchhiker's Guide to Monoculture: AI Homogenizes Syntax, Not (Necessarily) Semantics
candidates.task: Kaggle contest code submissions (2019 to mid-2026)
candidates.evidence: Within-contest similarity of submissions rises in surface syntax (TF-IDF) after AI coding assistants spread, but not in approach or intent (code embeddings); seeds converge on 42. Outside the science lane (software), kept for recall.

candidates.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Scientific Research: Individual Benefits, Collective Risks, and a Framework for Responsible Research with AI
candidates.task: Narrative review of evidence on generative AI across funding, research tasks, publication and peer review
candidates.evidence: Reviews the empirical literature and a workshop roundtable: productivity gains are well documented, while evidence on novelty, disruption and breakthrough output is ambiguous or negative; proposes a governance framework. Narrative review, not systematic.

candidates.title: AI and Its Impact on Creativity and Diversity: An Empirical Study of LLM-Generated Product Ideas
candidates.authors: Terwiesch, Meincke, Girotra, Mollick, Nave, Ulrich
candidates.task: New product ideas for college students priced under $50
candidates.evidence: Across eight studies, LLM ideas beat human ideas on purchase intent but are less novel individually and less diverse as a set; a re-analysis of earlier LLM creativity studies finds lower diversity throughout, and pooling vendors, prompting and agents push diversity toward human levels. May overlap with Girotra et al. (2023) and Meincke et al. (2024), which are already collected; outside the science lane.

candidates.title: Multi-agent AI systems outperform human teams in creativity
candidates.task: Six problem-solving ideation tasks (multi-agent LLM teams vs human teams)
candidates.evidence: Compares 4,541 multi-agent LLM ideas with 341 human-team ideas: LLM teams are more creative (d=1.50), driven by novelty with similar usefulness, and different conversation features predict creativity for each. Outside the science lane.

candidates.title: Where Models Converge and Humans Diverge: A Coverage Framework for Distributional Pluralism in Open-Ended Generation
candidates.task: Ideation and narrative tasks, including Harry Potter fan fiction (LLM vs human distributions)
candidates.evidence: Proposes coverage metrics grounded in the distribution of human writing on a topic; LLM output is plausible but narrow and concentrated near the center of the human response space. Outside the science lane.

candidates.title: Writing in Symbiosis: Mapping Human Creative Agency in the AI Era
candidates.task: Longitudinal creative-writing corpus spanning the pre- and post-LLM eras
candidates.evidence: Finds thematic convergence around AI topics alongside stylistic differentiation: some authors move toward AI style, some away, and some stay stable. Outside the science lane (creative writing).

candidates.title: Effects of Varying LLM Access on Essay Writing Behavior
candidates.task: College essay writing with no, limited, or unlimited LLM access
candidates.evidence: Pilot with 24 students in three access conditions: essay quality did not differ, but unlimited-access essays were closer to AI-generated text and those students reported less creative expression. The abstract does not state random assignment; outside the science lane.

candidates.title: Training Novices to Think, or Giving Them LLMs? Evidence from an RCT
candidates.task: Consultant-style recommendations for a university merchandising-shop business case
candidates.evidence: 2x2 RCT with 1,053 first-year undergraduates crossing ChatGPT Edu (GPT-4o) access with causal-reasoning training; ChatGPT raised expert evaluations and coherence, while the training (not ChatGPT) produced mechanism-based solutions and more unique ideas. The posting month comes from news coverage dated 2026-08-28; outside the science lane.

candidates.title: Does ChatGPT Help You Sell More? Effects of Large Language Models on Review Homogeneity and Product Sales
candidates.task: Amazon Electronics and Books product reviews (2021-2023)
candidates.evidence: Year-over-year difference-in-differences on about 5 million Amazon reviews shows semantic homogeneity rose after ChatGPT's release; a controlled study finds AI-generated reviews more homogeneous than human ones, and homogeneity has an inverted-U relation with sales. Outside the science lane.

candidates.title: The Syntactic Exoskeleton: How Generative AI Homogenizes the Structure of Arabic-L1 English Academic Writing
candidates.task: 423 essays by Arabic-L1 undergraduates (339 unassisted exam essays vs 84 GenAI-mediated assignments)
candidates.evidence: Comparative corpus study: GenAI-mediated essays compress sentence-length variance about eighteen-fold and lose L1 clause-chaining structure while scoring higher on CEFR proficiency. Not randomized; outside the science lane (education).

candidates.title: Semantic Similarity, Phrase Analysis, and Expert Evaluation of Human versus LLM-Generated Abstracts
candidates.task: Abstracts of 20 papers (Antioxidants, PLOS Computational Biology) vs ChatGPT and Qwen versions
candidates.evidence: AI-generated abstracts are more similar to one another (Jaccard about 0.66-0.68) than to author-written abstracts, and five experts rated AI abstracts higher on criteria including originality. Very small sample; one secondary page gave the issue as No. 3, but the journal's own page says Vol. 24, No. 1.

candidates.title: Large language models are homogeneously creative
other_versions: arXiv 2501.19361 (titled 'We're Different, We're the Same: Creative Homogeneity Across LLMs')
candidates.task: Standardized creativity tasks answered by many humans and many LLMs
candidates.evidence: Published version of an item already collected under its arXiv title: LLM responses resemble other LLMs' responses far more than human responses resemble each other, even after controlling for confounders.

candidates.title: How experience moderates the impact of AI suggestions on researchers' perceptions of their ideas
other_versions: doi 10.2139/ssrn.5013086 (titled 'How Experience Moderates the Impact of Generative AI Ideas on the Research Process')
candidates.task: Researchers' own research ideas with AI suggestions
candidates.evidence: Already in the collection; reported only to supply the Research Policy DOI and volume, which the collection lists as null. The design was not re-checked in this run; Crossref registered the SSRN version on 2025-01-08, and the collection lists a 2024 SSRN title.

candidates.title: The rise of large language models and the direction and impact of US federal research funding
candidates.authors: Qian, Wen, Furnas, Bai, Shao, Wang
candidates.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 123(33): e2601439123
candidates.task: NSF and NIH proposals from two R1 universities and all public NSF and NIH awards (2021-2025)
candidates.evidence: Already in the collection; listed with the published PNAS details (online 2026-08-11). Higher LLM involvement goes with lower semantic distinctiveness (closer to recently funded work); at NIH, LLM use predicts proposal success and more non-hit publications.

candidates.title: Quantifying large language model usage in scientific papers
other_versions: arXiv 2404.01268 (titled 'Mapping the Increasing Use of LLMs in Scientific Papers')
candidates.task: 950,965 papers on arXiv, bioRxiv and Nature portfolio journals (2020-2024)
candidates.evidence: Measures the prevalence of LLM-modified content over time; higher LLM modification goes with papers in more crowded research areas and shorter papers. No diversity outcome as such; listed as a prominent measurement study.

candidates.title: Delving into LLM-assisted writing in biomedical publications through excess vocabulary
other_versions: arXiv 2406.07016 (earlier title 'Delving into ChatGPT usage in academic writing through excess vocabulary')
candidates.task: 15 million PubMed abstracts (2010-2024)
candidates.evidence: Published version of an item already collected under its earlier title: excess-word analysis suggests at least 13.5% of 2024 biomedical abstracts were processed with LLMs. Measurement only, no diversity outcome.

candidates.title: ChatGPT "contamination": estimating the prevalence of LLMs in the scholarly literature
candidates.task: Scholarly literature published in 2023 (keyword prevalence)
candidates.evidence: Uses LLM-associated keywords to estimate that at least 60,000 papers (slightly over 1%) published in 2023 were LLM-assisted. Measurement only, no diversity outcome.

candidates.title: Is ChatGPT Transforming Academics' Writing Style?
candidates.task: One million arXiv abstracts (2018-2024)
candidates.evidence: A calibrated word-frequency model estimates that about 35% of computer-science abstracts show ChatGPT-revision style. Measurement only, no diversity outcome.

candidates.title: The diffusion of large language models in published academic articles
candidates.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 123(22): e2605754123
candidates.task: Full texts of 7.3 million articles from Elsevier, Frontiers, MDPI and PLoS (2020-2025)
candidates.evidence: Estimates that 57% of 2025 articles show LLM influence and that adoption is stratified by region, institution rank, publisher and field. Measurement only, no diversity outcome.

candidates.title: LLM-assisted proposal writing in competitive R&D funding: Evidence from Horizon Europe
candidates.venue: JRC Working Papers on Territorial Modelling and Analysis No. 02/2026
candidates.task: All firm applications to Horizon Europe (2021-2024)
candidates.evidence: About 40% of proposal abstracts show LLM-modified content by end-2024; heavy reliance correlates with lower scores, but within-firm resubmission analyses find no causal effect. No novelty or diversity outcome; listed as a grant-proposal measurement study.

candidates.title: Can LLM feedback enhance review quality? A randomized study of 20K reviews at ICLR 2025
candidates.task: Peer reviews at ICLR 2025 (over 20,000 reviews)
candidates.evidence: Submissions were randomized so that none, half, or all of their reviews got LLM feedback; reviewers who got feedback wrote longer, more specific and more actionable reviews, and 27% updated them. No creativity or diversity outcome, so likely out of scope.

candidates.title: Use and Effects of LLMs in Peer Review: A Randomized Experiment and Survey at ICML 2026
candidates.task: Peer reviewing at ICML 2026 under prohibitive vs permissive LLM policies
candidates.evidence: Reviewers (over 17,000, with 24,000+ papers) were randomly assigned to a policy banning LLM use or allowing limited help; effects on decisions, scores and confidence were minimal and permissive-policy reviews were 5.5-7% longer (survey N=1,486). No creativity or diversity outcome, so likely out of scope.

candidates.title: Human-AI Collaboration in Science at Scale: A Global Large-scale Randomized Field Experiment
candidates.task: LLM-generated feedback on arXiv preprints (31,000+ preprints, 45,000+ researchers)
candidates.evidence: Randomized delivery of LLM feedback to preprint authors raised the chance of revising the manuscript (12.55% relative increase) and later LLM use. No creativity or diversity outcome in the abstract, so likely out of scope.
